articles.title: Sunyshore had two chances. Stop arguing about the twelve points.
articles.dek: Mara Voss follows the last two Starseekers possessions and finds a defeat that cannot be explained by four opposing field goals.
articles.author: mara-voss

body.text: I don't want to hear that Sunyshore lost because Cerulean kicked four field goals. Of course the Tide kicked four field goals. Grotle made every attempt, the Starseekers scored six points, and arithmetic remains undefeated. Karson Jones needs a more useful conversation. His defense kept offering the offense a way out of a bad afternoon. Twice in the fourth quarter, Sunyshore moved the ball far enough to make that invitation serious. Twice, the possession ended without points.

That's where I'd start the meeting. At 3:36 remaining, trailing 12–6, Sunyshore began a possession that would cover 57 yards. After a fumble ended it, the defense immediately forced a punt. The next possession moved rapidly through three completed passes before failing on downs. Those are two distinct opportunities. Filing the entire loss under a vague complaint about offensive rhythm would let too many decisions escape inspection.

The first deserves particular attention because Sunyshore briefly found several different ways to advance. DeZhaun Watzon threw short middle to Swampert for ten yards. On third-and-one, a deep-right pass toward Floatzel was broken up by Raticate. Myles Gabite then took a fourth-and-one run left for eight. Scol Alexander ran up the middle for five and left for sixteen. The offense had a productive response to a failed throw. Good. Keep that part.

Then came the costly finish. Watzon completed a deep-right pass to Frigibax for nineteen yards. With 2:03 left, Scol Alexander ran left, lost two yards and fumbled. Shellder recovered for Cerulean. I won't invent a missed blocking assignment or announce that the ball carrier should have foreseen a particular tackle. The recorded sequence gives us enough: an offense finally joining its running and passing gains together lost the ball on first down.
It felt like finding the right door and dropping the key down the drain. We got another key, too. That part makes it harder to shrug at.
body.speaker: DeZhaun Watzon

body.text: The defense returned the favor

Cerulean took over with 2:02 remaining. Seismitoad lost a yard on a run right, lost another up the middle and then caught a short-right pass for two. Donphan made both rushing tackles; Vigoroth finished the reception. Grotle punted. That is a clean, useful defensive answer to a turnover. Sunyshore's offense had scarcely finished being disappointed before it was being asked to try again.

This is why I'm impatient with treating the result as a single blur of frustration. The Tide won without an offensive touchdown. Sunyshore held them to 28 rushing yards on 21 attempts. A defense can still make mistakes in a game like that, and Cerulean did convert six of sixteen third downs. But the final stop arrived exactly when it was needed. Jones had a game to win after the fumble.

At 1:47, Watzon found Floatzel short right for six. Three seconds later he hit Sceptile short right for 21. At 1:33, he went deep left to Floatzel for 26. Three completed passes, 53 yards before the ensuing failures, and a very different picture from the offense's earlier procession of punts. If you want evidence that this group could move against Cerulean, there it is. Nobody needs to borrow it from last week's score.

The next four throws were incomplete. Carnivine broke up consecutive passes intended for Swampert, the first short right and the second deep right. Maractus broke up the third-down deep-left attempt toward Finizen. The fourth-down short-right throw toward Frigibax also failed. Cerulean took over with 1:06 left and knelt twice. That is the end of the argument about whether there was still time.

I see a defense repeatedly contesting the catch, not a mystery that can be solved by yelling for more effort. Sunyshore finished ten of twenty-six passing, with three sacks and an interception. The Tide swatted nine passes. The final series supplied three named breakups in a row before the last incompletion. Any preparation for Mahogany that doesn't make those contested throws a central subject is missing the most legible evidence in the game.
Don't throw away the parts that worked

The temptation after six points is to declare every offensive choice defective. I wouldn't. Sunyshore ran for 82 yards on sixteen attempts. Myles Gabite's fourth-down conversion kept that first late drive alive. Scol Alexander's sixteen-yard run mattered before his fumble mattered. A ball-security correction should preserve the fact that the running game gave the offense useful distances and genuine progress.

Nor would I pretend every deep pass was reckless. Floatzel's 26-yard catch helped build the last chance. Frigibax's nineteen-yard reception helped build the previous one. The problem is deciding which opportunities remain sound when the defense is already getting hands on so many throws. That is a question for Jones and Watzon to answer with specific routes and protections in practice, rather than a blanket instruction to become more adventurous or more cautious.

Cerulean deserves credit for the less dramatic work, too. Farigiraf was not sacked. The Tide did not throw an interception or lose a fumble. Grotle connected from 25, forty, 36 and 24 yards. A team that protects its possessions and takes every available kick can beat a more celebrated opponent without producing the afternoon's loudest play. Misty's club moved above .500 at 4–3 by doing precisely that.

Sunyshore remains 5–2, with 181 points scored and 92 allowed. I'm not tearing up that record because one afternoon went sour. I am rejecting the idea that a good season makes the final two possessions unimportant. Contenders need a response more exact than reassurance. They need to retain the gains, correct the failures and know which of those two categories each play belongs in.

Mahogany arrives next. The Frost just protected a one-point lead by finishing their last possession with consecutive productive runs before kneeling. Sunyshore has its own closing sequence to repair. Put four clips next to the 53 yards that preceded them: broken up, broken up, broken up, incomplete. Start there.

articles.title: Close is a score. It is not a diagnosis.
articles.dek: Ellis Quill visits four narrow defeats and argues that the next useful question depends on how each team lost its last chance.
articles.author: ellis-quill

body.text: I have a modest objection to the phrase “one play away.” It is usually true, which makes it very convenient. A team loses by one, two, three or four points, and everyone can select a moment that would have changed the answer. The phrase then sits comfortably between disappointment and hope, asking almost nothing of either. After this week's games, I'd rather ask what the team has to practice.

Rustboro lost by four. Petalburg lost by three. Celadon lost by two. Fortree lost by one. That is a tidy little staircase, although I doubt any of the coaches would appreciate the design. The scores suggest four clubs standing near the same door. The possessions tell a more useful story. They have arrived there by different routes, and some have quite different reasons for being unable to open it.

Start with Rustboro, because Tyler Scarboro's team has plenty of evidence that the basic work of moving the ball was possible. The Stone gained 334 yards against Azalea's 260. They made nineteen first downs to eleven and converted six of twelve third downs. My Way, Son ran for 109 yards. Anyone announcing that the offense could do nothing is going to have an awkward conversation with the first three quarters.

Yet Rustboro scored ten points, all before halftime. Its final two substantial drives ended on downs. With four minutes left, a fourth-and-four short-left pass to Lombre was broken up by Castform. After Azalea went ahead, the Stone returned with another long possession. They converted a fourth-and-one run through Watchog. On the next fourth down, needing five with 1:02 remaining, My Way, Son ran left for no gain. Kricketune made the tackle.
The hundred yards don't cancel that last carry. They also don't disappear because of it. We can work with both things without pretending either one didn't happen.
body.speaker: My Way, Son

body.text: That seems a sensible place for Scarboro to begin. The nine-yard run that ended in a first-half fumble also belongs in the review. Rustboro had enough movement to make several endings painful. The work is to finish those possessions, protect the ball and choose a convincing answer when the distance becomes non-negotiable. “Keep doing everything” is too gentle. “Change everything” would discard the useful parts.
A comeback that never got another turn

Petalburg's 17–14 defeat at Mt. Silver had a different shape. Norman's team reached the end zone on fourth-and-five with two minutes left, Iron Valiant throwing short left to Girafarig for fourteen yards. That was a successful answer at the very moment Rustboro's last drive had lacked one. It gave the Pride a three-point deficit and something worth trying to recover.

The ensuing onside kick went to Mt. Silver. Then Raticate ran right for three, Vibrava ran left for ten and Vibrava caught a short-left pass for twelve. The Reds knelt twice. Petalburg never got to run the next urgent offensive series. It is tempting to spend all the sympathy on the touchdown and all the blame on the kick, but the defensive chance after the recovery matters as well. The Reds still had to collect the yards that ended the contest.

I don't often volunteer applause for Mt. Silver, whose unbeaten record already seems to find sufficient publicity. That final sequence deserves a little. Three different gains, then the quiet finish. For Petalburg, the useful question is how to force the opponent to surrender one more possession. The Pride also punted six times. A late touchdown can be admirable while the preceding work leaves too much for it to solve.

At 5–2, Petalburg can take the bye without turning a three-point loss into an identity crisis. Norman has an offense that produced two passing touchdowns against an unbeaten opponent. He also has specific stretches in which that offense went nowhere. The review needs room for both. I would be wary of any meeting in which the fourth-quarter rally receives all the attention simply because it is easiest to remember kindly.
One point can contain several jobs

Fortree's loss was smaller and its situation more severe. The Skyhawks fell to 0–6 after Chinchou's 53-yard field goal cut Mahogany's lead to 14–13. It was a fine kick. It was also the final time Fortree possessed the ball. When I hear “one point away” in that context, I want to know what happened after the kick, because another successful kick requires another opportunity.

Bibarel ran right for six and then seven. Kricketune followed with runs up the middle for six and ten. Mahogany knelt twice. There is the immediate problem in four ordinary handoffs. Earlier in the quarter, Kingdra had taken consecutive sacks for eight and seven yards, turning an advancing Fortree drive into a punt. Winona has protection to review and a late run defense to repair. The kicker's distance does not make either subject smaller.

Celadon's ending was even longer. The Bloom punted early in the fourth quarter while trailing Canalave 9–7. The Bulwark then held the ball for the remaining 5:12. Grotle converted a fourth-and-one run up the middle for five. Slowking later found Delcatty for ten on third-and-six, then Manectric for eight on second-and-six. Two kneels ended it. Erika never received the last possession that a two-point deficit seems to promise.

The Bloom had managed only six first downs and 167 total yards. Their missed field goal belongs in the explanation, but asking for a better kick cannot be the entire improvement plan. The defense needed one more stop; the offense needed to manufacture more chances before the last five minutes vanished. At 1–6, Celadon needs practical work more than another beautifully phrased reminder of how nearly this one went differently.

These are not four versions of the same football team. Rustboro is 3–4, Petalburg 5–2, Celadon 1–6 and Fortree 0–6. Their next weeks differ, too: the Pride rest, while the Stone visit Viridian, the Bloom visit Fuchsia and the Skyhawks host Vermilion. Encouragement should be specific enough to travel with each team into that next assignment.

I'd tell Rustboro to remember that its last drive reached two fourth downs and answered only one. I'd tell Petalburg that finishing its own touchdown drive still left a defensive job. I'd ask Celadon and Fortree to study the runs and completions that denied them another try. There is hope in close games. There is also a practice schedule. Four yards, three points, two kneels, one more stop: pick the thing your team can actually work on.

articles.title: Blackthorn, keep the ball in Hatterene’s hands.
articles.dek: Dorian Pike counts five touchdown passes, admires an eighty-yard answer to a sack and demands that the Dragons remember what made 42 possible.
articles.author: dorian-pike

body.text: I would like to begin with a respectful acknowledgment of restraint. A club at 5–1 should avoid getting carried away by one emphatic victory. Its coaches should study the mistakes. Its quarterback should thank the blockers. Its receivers should remember that the next game begins at zero. There. The responsible sentences have been completed. Blackthorn won 42–0, Hatterene threw for 410 yards, and I would now like someone to explain why the Dragons should whisper about it.

Five touchdown passes. Thirty completions in 35 attempts. Zero interceptions. Clair's offense gave six different receivers a catch and four different receivers a touchdown. Ninjask had 183 receiving yards; Grovyle caught nine passes. This was a passing game with a devastating lead performer and enough support to keep the entire production from becoming one very long solo.

And here's the uncomfortable truth: the most revealing play came immediately after Blackthorn did something wrong. Hatterene took a sack, leaving second-and-seventeen. With 2:15 left in the second quarter, the next throw went deep middle to Ninjask for an eighty-yard touchdown. Eighty. An offense that can respond to a seven-yard loss by traveling eighty on one completion does not need a lecture about how comforting it would be to run twice and punt politely.

That doesn't excuse the sack. It changes the response available after it. Clair has a quarterback and receiver who turned a bad distance into the afternoon's longest play. I want that confidence to remain part of the plan. If next week's meeting converts a spectacular win into an invitation to become timid, someone should bring the eighty-yard clip and play it at an irritating volume.
Second-and-seventeen sounds wonderfully official. Then Ninjask is running and you start wondering whether the defense filled out the wrong paperwork.
body.speaker: Hatterene

body.text: The short pass joined the argument

The next touchdown to Ninjask traveled 37 yards on a throw described as short middle. It came with 45 seconds left before halftime. This is an important detail for anyone who believes the entire afternoon can be explained by launching the ball farther. The Dragons found an enormous play on a deep throw and another on a short one. The receiver helped turn both into seven points after the conversion.

Ninjask caught seven of eight targets. The eighty-yarder is allowed to attract the spotlight; it has earned the electricity bill. But the seven catches matter because the offense could keep returning to that receiver without requiring every play to be historic. A reliable completion and an explosive finish are pleasant things to find in the same uniform. I recommend that Blackthorn continue taking advantage of the arrangement.

Grovyle supplied nine catches on ten targets for 78 yards. One was the one-yard touchdown that opened the scoring. A receiver who can finish the close work and keep appearing on ordinary downs is doing a different job from the player with the eighty-yard score. Both jobs were necessary to the way this offense distributed its opportunities. The biggest number should not make the other work invisible.

Exploud caught all five targets for 34 yards and a touchdown. Seadra caught both targets for 27 and a touchdown. Furret caught all three for 24. Meganium added four receptions for 64. That is a receiving list with enough names to interrupt the comfortable habit of blaming one matchup for everything. Blackthorn kept finding somewhere useful to put the ball.
The long one counts. So do the catches that give us another set of downs. I'll take the throw that's there and keep running until the play is finished.
body.speaker: Ninjask

body.text: I appreciate the practicality. I also reserve the right to be less calm about eighty yards. Someone on this staff has to enjoy the numbers without immediately wrapping them in a blanket and asking whether they're getting too warm. Ninjask gained more receiving yards than the opposing offense gained total yards. That happened. We can say it at full volume.
A shutout deserves its own paragraph

Several paragraphs, actually. Blackthorn allowed 169 total yards and just 66 through the air. The opposition converted two of eleven third downs and punted seven times. No interception was required to manufacture that shutout. No lost opposing fumble was required either. The Dragons repeatedly made the ordinary defensive sequence work: contest the gain, force the difficult down and get off the field.

Leavanny recorded two sacks. James Harriolu and Beedrill had one each. Politoed made seven tackles, while Whiscash added four and a tackle for loss. A 42-point offense can make every defensive contribution seem like an optional decoration. I object. Those stops helped ensure that Hatterene's success kept widening the game instead of merely answering the next score.

There are corrections available. Blackthorn allowed 103 rushing yards on nineteen carries. Hatterene was sacked three times. The Dragons converted only three of eight third downs and punted three times. Clair can have all those details without surrendering the larger point. Forty-two to nothing is not a fragile result that shatters when somebody mentions a missed opportunity. It can survive inspection.

The protection figures suggest where some of that inspection belongs. Bellibolt allowed five pressures, and Lickilickelce allowed three and a sack. That does not identify every individual assignment on the scoring throws, so I won't pretend it does. It does give the line a concrete subject for work. The quarterback's completion rate should be an achievement the blockers help sustain, not an excuse to ignore the times defenders got through.
Five wins still require a plan

Blackthorn has scored 120 points and allowed 77 across six games. This one result supplied 42 of those points and none of the concessions. That proportion is both exciting and demanding. I cannot honestly promise that this is the offensive output the Dragons will reproduce every week. I can insist that the staff understand exactly which opportunities made it possible before congratulating itself and moving on.

Keep the variety of receiving jobs. Keep the willingness to attack after a setback. Keep the short completions that allow a gifted receiver to make the next defender's afternoon unpleasant. Fix the protection leaks and the wasted third downs. Those instructions can coexist. The idea that ambition and correction must take turns in the same meeting is how good football teams spend too long congratulating themselves on being sensible.

Clair has a 5–1 club and a quarterback who just completed thirty throws. The obligation is to give that quarterback more good decisions to make. When the next second-and-seventeen arrives, remember that Blackthorn has already answered one with Hatterene, Ninjask and eighty yards through the middle.
